court: SUPREME COURT OF THE STATE OF NEW YORK · COUNTY OF NEW YORK
caption: Jane Doe v. Cornell University, Inc., et al.
lead: On the evening of October 19, 2024, a [20-year-old](cbs-details) Cornell undergraduate, identified in court papers as Jane Doe, drank vodka at her Delta Delta Delta sorority house, then went with sorority sisters to a chapter event at Moonies Bar & Nightclub and on to a second downtown bar. At about 11 p.m. she left alone and walked to the Chi Phi (Xi Chapter) fraternity house at 107 Edgemoor Lane to see her friend Matthew Ingalls. By then, the complaint says, she had consumed about ten drinks in three hours and was visibly intoxicated ([¶¶ 135–144](complaint@23)).

Her civil complaint alleges that inside the house she was pressured into snorting ketamine for the first time, given marijuana and a high-proof "Jamaican liquor," and then sexually assaulted by seven fraternity members. At about 1:42 a.m. one of them allegedly announced in the chapter's "Chi Phi Actives" Snapchat group that there was "free pussy" upstairs ([¶ 162](complaint@26)), after which more members came into the room. The complaint says she was "completely incapacitated" by the final assault, which ended at about 5:45 a.m., when she lost consciousness ([¶¶ 152–174](complaint@25)).
defendantsIntro: The complaint names eighteen defendants in its [caption](complaint@3): the university, the fraternity's national and chapter entities, her own sorority, the bar that served her while she was under 21, the seven students she says assaulted her, the Chi Phi chapter president, and unnamed faculty, alumni and chapter officers.

notices: Every account of the night on this page comes from the plaintiff's civil complaint or from published reporting. These are allegations: none has been proven in court, and as of October 2, 2026, none of the seven men has been charged with a crime ([CBS](cbs-details)).
Several defendants deny the allegations through counsel. Cornell's Title IX process reached split outcomes, and Cornell has not said which outcome applied to which student ([Cornell FAQ](cu-faq)).

closing: This case is multi-faceted. To start, how was an underage girl, marked as underage with Xs by the bouncer, able to get served at Moonies Bar? And what does Moonies claim? Just that alone is complicated, because [her testimony does not match the videos](da). There is evidence that during the event, and for 2-3 weeks after, Jane Doe told colleagues and Cornell University Police Department (CUPD) officers that [nothing illegal, nothing non-consensual took place](da), and that, in her own words, [she even enjoyed the experience](cbs-texts). But, as expected during intense traumatic experiences like this, her narrative shifts a lot. A month after the event, [when she talks to CUPD](cbs-texts), this is when she decides she was assaulted and permanently changes her narrative. Only after she learns of the [group chat](cbs-snap), only after she hears rumors spreading around the campus. Only when she can't go to class anymore, can't go to parties, can't open social media without seeing something, can't have friends without being mocked, only then do the [Manhattan lawyers](complaint@101) and [national media cameras](nyt) appear.

Every day 1500 people get sexually assaulted. As a person who has been assaulted, and did not have the same fortune of an entire nation's media spotlight, I am just trying to find some truth here. In a case primarily made up of one-sided hearsay. For the sake of all of us, who had no choice but to just wake up the next day. And wake up the day after that.

So, what is the definition of consent? Is it sexual assault if the parties involved express consent during the act and for weeks after, but a month later change their mind? Does the trauma warrant a window of time, or is that window a weapon? My thoughts also go to the negligence of the NY Supreme Court, who have granted anonymity for Jane Doe, but [publicly released the names of the 7 investigated kids](complaint@3), when nothing has been proven or decided yet. Their lives are ruined, for life, regardless of the outcome of this case. They've lost their jobs and won't be able to get any others, because as soon as you Google their names, this appears. Even if they're acquitted, it's game over for their professional careers, and their public lives. This is the case for all 7 of them, even though 2 in particular are far more culpable than the other 5. And another 2 even testify they did nothing but [walk in the room, check on Jane Doe, and walk out](da). Yet their outcomes are all the same, a permanent black mark on their lives, forever. The internet is even going so far as hurting those with the same names as them, completely innocent lives, also hurt.

So what is fair here? This site is an independent attempt at consolidating the news, at being impartial. But just by the nature of communication, being fully impartial is impossible. Read through and decide for yourself.
